title: Bifunctional Nickel and Copper Electrocatalysts for CO2 Reduction and the Oxygen Evolution Reaction
abstract: In this study, a bifunctional electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction and the O2 evolution reaction (OER) was constructed from the electrodeposition of cuprous oxide (Cu2O) and Ni on a carbon substrate. Different Ni thicknesses on Cu2O were achieved by varying the time of chronopotentiometric deposition of Ni. Electrochemical CO2 reduction was carried out at -0.89 V and -1.89 V vs. RHE, and it was found that formate and CO were the two major products. Cu2O modified with a Ni overlayer with a thickness of ~700 nm resulted in the highest formate Faradaic efficiency of 18%, and Cu2O resulted in highest CO Faradaic efficiency of 7.9%. The enhanced Faradaic efficiency for formate is attributed to the synergistic effect between Ni and Cu2O due to maximized amounts of exposed bimetallic sites that facilitate CO2 reduction. The electrocatalyst also produces ~9 times more current density than previous studies using Ni-Cu2O electrocatalysts for the OER. The ability of the Ni-Cu2O thin films to catalyze both the OER and CO2 reduction allows them to be incorporated in the first demonstration of a two-electrode CO2 conversion device with a bifunctional catalyst. In this architecture, the device produces formate and CO with Faradaic efficiencies of 16.0% and 19.7%, respectively. sections.heading: Bifunctional Nickel and Copper Electrocatalysts for CO2 Reduction and the Oxygen Evolution Reaction
sections.text:
In this study, a bifunctional electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction and the O2 evolution reaction
(OER) was constructed from the electrodeposition of cuprous oxide (Cu2O) and Ni on a carbon substrate. Different Ni thicknesses on Cu2O were achieved by varying the time of chronopotentiometric deposition of Ni. Electrochemical CO2 reduction was carried out at -0.89 V and -1.89 V vs. RHE, and it was found that formate and CO were the two major products. Cu2O modified with a Ni overlayer with a thickness of ~700 nm resulted in the highest formate Faradaic
efficiency of 18%, and Cu2O resulted in highest CO Faradaic efficiency of 7.9%. The enhanced Faradaic efficiency for formate is attributed to the synergistic effect between Ni and Cu2O due to maximized amounts of exposed bimetallic sites that facilitate CO2 reduction. The electrocatalyst also produces ~9 times more current density than previous studies using Ni-Cu2O electrocatalysts for the OER. The ability of the Ni-Cu2O thin films to catalyze both the OER and CO2 reduction allows them to be incorporated in the first demonstration of a two-electrode CO2 conversion device with a bifunctional catalyst. In this architecture, the device produces formate and CO with Faradaic
efficiencies of 16.0% and 19.7%, respectively.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
The global average atmospheric CO2 concentration in June 2019 was 413.0 ± 0.1 ppm, a level higher than at any point in the previous 800,000 years.1 To mitigate rising CO2 levels and the resulting effects of climate change, a number of technologies to reduce CO2 emissions have been investigated such as carbon capture and storage and carbon capture and conversion. Conversion technologies aim to capture atmospheric CO2 and subsequently convert it to value-added products.2 Electrochemical CO2 reduction offers a viable route to convert CO2 into fuel or chemical feedstocks. Electrochemical CO2 reduction on various metal electrodes was pioneered by Hori in the 1980’s.3,4,5,6 Since then, Cu electrodes have been widely studied as effective CO2 reduction electrocatalysts that are capable of producing hydrocarbon products with reasonable Faradaic efficiencies.4,5,7,8 However, major drawbacks of Cu electrodes are that they are limited by the large overpotential (> 0.7 V) required for CO2 reduction to outcompete H2O reduction and that their selectivity among carbon products is less than ideal.9 Therefore, to improve Cu electrodes, the catalysts must be modified to produce active sites that are different from those of a pure Cu surface. Metal oxides provide one possible way to achieve these different active sites.10,11,12 For example, Li et al. prepared thin films of Cu2O by annealing Cu foil in air and electrochemically reducing the resulting Cu2O layers. These Cu2O films exhibited current densities of 1 mA/cm2 at overpotentials < 0.4 V and a higher level of activity than pure Cu electrodes.13 Albo et al. constructed Cu2O-loaded gas diffusion electrodes capable of electrochemically reducing CO2 to CO at 54.8% efficiency.14 Kas et al. reported on the selectivity of Cu2O thin films for ethane, ethylene, methane, and CO, which is highly dependent on film thickness.15 Chang et al.

3 synthesized Cu2O cubes to electrochemically reduce CO2 at a potential range of 0 to -1.7 V vs. SCE and showed methanol to be the dominant product.16 Ohya et al. studied the electrochemical reduction of CO2 using Zn particles mixed with CuO and Cu2O powders. They found that the copper oxide catalysts were selective for ethylene in a methanol electrolyte.17 Yuan reported that a hybrid catalyst consisting of Cu2O and TiO2 electrochemically reduces CO2 to ethanol, acetone, and n-propanol with a maximum Faradaic efficiency of 47.4%.18 Ren et al. described the selective electroreduction of CO2 to ethylene and ethanol using Cu2O films. They found that the Faradaic yields of ethylene and ethanol can be tuned by varying the film thickness.19 Lastly, Malik et al. evaluated CO2 reduction to methanol using multi-walled carbon nanotubes impregnated with Cu2O with a Faradaic efficiency of 38%.20 Our group recently demonstrated that electrodeposited Cu2O thin films modified with a Ni overlayer on tin-doped indium oxide (ITO) substrates enhanced O2 evolution reaction (OER) performance in alkaline solution.21 By varying the amount of electrodeposited Ni, we were able to tune the catalytic activity of these thin films. The best catalyst had an average Ni thickness of 3.2 µm and exhibited an onset overpotential of only 150 mV.21 This work demonstrated that the OER activity of Cu2O can be improved by adding varying amounts of Ni. Based on these results, we hypothesize that these bimetallic Ni-Cu2O composites would be an efficient CO2 reduction electrocatalyst. Since Cu2O is a good CO2 reduction catalyst, we speculated that we could enhance Cu2O performance by adding a Ni overlayer. Furthermore, we hypothesize that these Ni-Cu2O composites have the ability to behave as a bifunctional catalyst since they exhibit excellent OER activity. Most bifunctional electrocatalysts reported in literature have the ability to enhance water splitting for generating H2, and they facilitate both the OER and H2 evolution reaction.22,23,24,25 To

4 the best of our knowledge, a bifunctional catalyst that performs CO2 reduction and OER has not been previously reported. In this manuscript, we report the facile synthesis of a novel bimetallic and bifunctional electrocatalyst that facilitates the OER and CO2 reduction. One benefit of a bifunctional electrocatalyst is the ability to catalyze both the OER and CO2 reduction on the same electrode when the applied potentials are switched between oxidative and reductive conditions.26,27,28 This switching feature could increase catalyst durability by preventing degradative overoxidation or overreduction at each electrode. Additionally, because the same material is used on both electrodes, bifunctional catalysts would increase the simplicity of designing practical CO2 reduction electrolyzers. Most research on Ni OER catalysts is performed at pH 14, but in this work we demonstrate that a Ni-based catalyst exhibits good performance under typical CO2 reduction conditions (pH = 6.8). These thin films are fabricated via the electrodeposition of varying amounts of Ni on a layer of Cu2O on a carbon substrate. We highlight carbon as a solid support because of its stability and durability. Furthermore, it is a low-cost and abundant material that possesses high surface area, which supports high current densities. The Ni-Cu2O catalysts are selective for formate and CO over other carbon products. We propose that the enhanced CO2 reduction activity is a result of the synergistic interaction between Ni and Cu in the bimetallic electrocatalyst.

All chemicals were used without further purification. Chronoamperometric Electrodeposition of Cuprous Oxide. Cu2O was electrodeposited onto carbon paper (Fuel Cell Store, AvCarb EP40T) at 50 °C for 30 min using a modified published procedure.29 A three-electrode electrochemical cell was used with carbon paper as the working electrode, Cu foil as the counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl (3 M KCl, eDaq, Inc.) as the reference electrode. The Cu2O electrodeposition bath contained 0.66 M CuSO4 and 7.5 M lactic acid adjusted to pH 12 with NaOH. The electrodeposition was carried out in the dark using a voltage of -0.45 V vs. Ag/AgCl. The thin films were left to dry in air and rinsed with water to remove residual CuSO4 on the surface. Chronopotentiometric Electrodeposition of Nickel. Ni was electrodeposited on the Cu2O thin films at room temperature in a three-electrode cell with a Pt wire counter electrode. The Ni electrodeposition bath contained 0.4 M boric acid and 0.5 M NiSO4 that was adjusted to pH 3 using H2SO4. To electrodeposit different thicknesses of Ni films, chronopotentiometry at -4 mA/cm2 was performed for varying time periods. The Ni-Cu2O thin films were left to dry in air before use. Electrochemical Measurements and Material Characterization. All electrochemical measurements were performed using a VSP-300 Biologic Potentiostat. All electrochemical data were collected versus a Ag/AgCl reference electrode and converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale. All voltage values are reported versus RHE. To evaluate the CO2 reduction activity of the thin films, the working electrodes were studied in 0.1 M sodium bicarbonate buffer sparged with CO2 gas (or N2 gas for control experiments) for at least 30 min using a three-electrode

To test the bifunctionality (OER and CO2 reduction) of the thin films, the working electrodes were studied in the same bicarbonate buffer sparged with CO2 gas in a one-compartment, two-electrode configuration. The working electrode consisted of the Ni-Cu2O catalyst produced using 100 s of Ni electrodeposition, and the counter electrode consisted of the Ni-Cu2O catalyst produced using 200s of Ni electrodeposition. Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images and energy-dispersive X-ray (EDS) analysis were obtained for each sample using a JEOL JSM6010LA analytical SEM or a JEOL JSM-7100F field emission SEM operated using an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was conducted using a Rigaku Smartlab diffractometer with a Cu Kα X-ray source. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed using a PHI model 5600 spectrometer using monochromatic Al Kα radiation with an 800 m diameter area of analysis. Product Determination. Electrochemical reactions were performed chronoamperometrically at - 0.89 V and -1.89 V vs. RHE for one hour using carbon as a counter electrode in a beaker for determining liquid and solid products or in a custom-made cell for determining gas products (Figure S1, ESI). The working electrode had an area of 5 cm2. During chronoamperometry, CO2 was continuously sparged through the solution (2.5 mL) at a rate of 5 cm3/min. Liquid and solid products were quantified using a Varian 400 MHz NMR Spectrometer. For formate quantification, the water in the reaction solution was evaporated under reduced pressure, and sodium formate along with other residual solids from the electrolyte were collected and dissolved in D2O. A representative NMR spectrum is shown in Figure S2, ESI. Liquid products were extracted from the reaction solution using deuterated chloroform. Gas products were quantified using a SRI 8610C gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) and a methanizer. sections.heading: CO2 Reduction by Ni-Cu2O Thin Films
sections.text:
The electrocatalysts were fabricated by the electrodeposition of Cu2O on carbon paper by modifying a previously reported procedure.29 Lactic acid is added to the Cu electrodeposition solution because lactate is a complexing agent that solubilizes Cu(II) ions under the alkaline conditions of the electrodeposition bath. During electrodeposition, the Cu(II) in the lactate complex is reduced to Cu(I), which forms insoluble Cu2O on the electrode surface.30,31 Ni was then electrodeposited on top of Cu2O chronopotentiometrically at -4 mA/cm2 as reported by Lee et al.21 By varying the electrodeposition time (10 s, 20 s, 100 s, 160 s, 200 s, and 500 s), the thickness of the Ni overlayer can be tuned (Table 1). Since the carbon substrate used is porous and the catalysts are highly heterogeneous, the thickness values in this table merely represent the average thicknesses across the catalysts as calculated from coulometry.

At voltages between -0.5 V and -1.0 V, more current is generated when the electrodes are studied under CO2 demonstrating that CO2 is indeed being reduced. The significant amount of cathodic current density under N2, however, indicates that the thin films also generate H2. Figure 2a presents LSVs of Cu2O, a Ni overlayer on Cu2O produced via 500 s of Ni electrodeposition, and a carbon substrate without Cu2O that is modified only by conducting Ni electrodeposition for 500 s. The electrode with 500 s worth of Ni electrodeposition on carbon without Cu2O generates a relatively small amount of current density (-1.9 mA/cm2 at -1.4 V) and less than that produced by polycrystalline Ni (Figure S3, ESI, red line). Polycrystalline Cu generates a current density of -8 mA/cm2 at -1.4 V (Figure S3, ESI, grey line), which is less than that of Cu2O at -12 mA/cm2 at the same voltage (Figure 2a, grey line). Cu2O also exhibits an earlier onset potential of -0.2 V as compared to an onset potential of -0.5 V for Cu. LSVs of catalysts with 20 s, 100 s, 160 s, and 200 s Ni electrodeposition times all have similar shapes to that of Cu2O (Figure S3, ESI). In contrast, the shape of the LSV when 500 s of Ni is electrodeposited is similar to that of polycrystalline Ni, demonstrating that the large amount of Ni electrodeposited causes it to behave similarly to a pure Ni substrate. Figure 2b shows the current density produced by different catalysts at -0.59 V vs. RHE. The electrode produced using 200 s of Ni electrodeposition on Cu2O generates the most current of -6.4 mA/cm2. Taken together, these data demonstrate that the electrochemical behavior of the Ni-Cu2O catalysts changes with increasing amounts of Ni and that there is an optimal amount of Ni electrodeposition for maximum catalyst current density.

and 3.8% formate, respectively. Our FE for Cu foil at -0.89 V is similar to that previously reported

In an effort to understand their structure and function, we characterized the Ni-Cu2O
catalysts using X-ray diffraction (XRD), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and scanning
electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The XRD pattern
(Figure 4) of a carbon electrode modified with Cu2O and 20 s of Ni electrodeposition exhibits several peaks attributed to the carbon support, which has been treated with a
polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) polymer, the (110), (111), and (220) facets of Cu2O, and the (111) and (220) facets of Ni. Figure 5 presents the Cu and Ni portions of the XPS spectrum of the carbon
electrode modified with Cu2O and 20 s of Ni electrodeposition. For the Cu region (Figure 5a), the two most intense peaks correspond to Cu2p1/2 and Cu2p3/2 transitions. These two peaks have binding energies that match well with literature values for Cu2O.32 It is difficult using XPS to differentiate between the presence of Cu2O and Cu because the binding energies are nearly identical. However, since the XRD spectrum does not show any evidence of Cu, the two prominent
peaks in the Cu portion of the XPS spectrum can be ascribed to Cu2O, not Cu. The minor peaks labeled A-D in the Cu portion of the spectrum match with the reported values for CuO, indicating
that the catalysts also contain a minor amount of CuO impurity. The Ni region of the XPS spectrum

To investigate why an optimal amount of Ni electrodeposition maximizes the catalytic
yield of formate and to verify the composition of the Ni-Cu2O films, SEM-EDS analysis was performed. Carbon paper is a web-like fibrous material with spindles along which Cu2O grows (Figure 6a). These Cu2O clusters serve as nucleation sites for Ni to grow during electrodeposition (Figures 6b-f). Since the Ni-Cu2O catalyst formed using 20 s of Ni electrodeposition was found to produce the highest FE for formate, SEM-EDS mapping of this catalyst was conducted (Figure 7).
The overall EDS spectrum (Figure 7b) contains peaks associated with Cu, F, O, Ni, and S. Cu, O,
and Ni come from the Ni and Cu2O thin films, S originates from NiSO4 used in the Ni electrodeposition bath, and F comes from the carbon substrate since it has been treated with PTFE
to render the carbon surface hydrophobic.34 The presence of PTFE was verified through EDS
mapping of pure carbon, in which both the spectrum and map show fluorine as a major component
(Figure S5, ESI). Elemental maps of the catalyst show that Cu2O grows along the carbon fibers in clusters. The fairly uniform distribution of Ni on the Cu2O (Figure 7f) leads to a high number of bimetallic Cu-Ni sites, which we hypothesize result in the higher FE for formate. Previous
calculations have determined that the binding energy of oxygen to Cu-Ni bimetallic sites is
significantly higher than that to monometallic Cu sites.35 A greater oxygen binding energy for Cu-
Ni sites favors the formation of a Cu-Ni-OCOH intermediate over the carbon-bound isomer (Cu-
Ni-COOH). The preference for Cu-Ni to form the oxygen bound intermediate could explain the
tendency for the Ni-Cu2O catalysts to produce more formate than CO at -0.89 V for RHE whereas the Cu2O catalyst without a Ni overlayer produces a greater proportion of CO (Figure 3a). Indeed, analogous intermediates supported by oxophilicity measurements have been invoked to explain
trends in formate and CO selectivity for Fe and Co CO2 reduction catalysts.36 EDS mapping of the Cu2O on carbon electrode produced using 500 s of Ni electrodeposition shows that there is

Figure 8 compares electrodes of Cu2O and Cu2O modified with 100 s of Ni
electrodeposition on carbon paper versus ITO. In our previous study, Cu2O and Ni-Cu2O were deposited on top of an ITO substrate and evaluated for their OER behavior.21 Comparing the OER
activity of Cu2O and Ni-Cu2O on ITO and carbon, current density is enhanced about 9-fold when the catalysts are deposited on carbon substrates. This finding demonstrates the superiority of
carbon as a solid support as opposed to ITO. Furthermore, ITO degrades rapidly under the very
negative potentials at which CO2 reduction occurs.37 Therefore, we highlight carbon as a stable and durable material that is abundant, low-cost, and environmentally benign. In Figure 9, the
bifunctionality of the electrocatalyst is tested in a one-compartment, two-electrode configuration
with the Cu2O electrode modified with 100 s of Ni electrodeposition as the working electrode and the Cu2O electrode modified with 200 s of Ni electrodeposition as the counter electrode. The device was polarized from 0 to 2.1 V in 0.1 M NaHCO3 sparged with CO2. A control experiment was performed with two carbon substrates as working and counter electrodes, in which very low
current densities were produced. When a further control experiment conducted with buffer sparged
with N2, less current density was produced when compared to the system studied under CO2. These two control experiments demonstrate that CO2 is indeed reduced in a practical two-electrode device architecture and that the Ni-Cu2O catalysts are responsible for facilitating both CO2 reduction and O2 evolution. Based on the standard half-cell potentials for CO2 reduction to formate (E° = -0.2 V vs. RHE)38 and O2 evolution (E° = +1.23 V vs. RHE)39, the thermodynamic potential for a two-electrode device producing formate and O2 is 1.43 V. We observe an onset potential near this 1.43 V theoretical value, signifying that the two-electrode device with the Ni-Cu2O catalysts exhibits a very low onset overpotential (Figure 9a, red line). In addition, the effectiveness of the
bifunctional device is demonstrated by its ability to produce formate and CO at reasonably high

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text:
In conclusion, Ni-Cu2O bifunctional electrocatalysts were fabricated and evaluated for the
CO2 reduction and O2 evolution reactions. For electrocatalytic CO2 reduction, formate and CO were the major products produced with FEs of 16.0% and 19.7% in a two-electrode device. The
enhanced catalytic activity of the Ni-Cu2O thin films is due to the synergistic effect of Ni and Cu2O and the maximized number of bimetallic active sites made available by the porous carbon substrate.
Whereas a Cu2O catalyst without Ni preferentially forms CO over formate at -0.89 V vs. RHE, the addition of a Ni overlayer switches that preference to formate at the same voltage. The catalysts
are also durable and function for 24 hours at an overpotential of ~0.67 V in a practical two-
electrode configuration. Future work will evaluate other bimetallic catalysts produced via
electrodeposition that can further enhance CO2 reduction and O2 evolution. Author Information Corresponding Author *E-mail: cbarile@unr.edu Notes
